newsitem.title: UK: Pig transplants delayed in Britain - newspaper.
newsitem.headline: Pig transplants delayed in Britain - newspaper.

text.p: The British government has delayed the first scheduled transplants of pig organs into people for fear of deadly animal viruses, the Times newspaper reports.

It says a government-appointed committee is holding off on publishing a report on the possible benefits and risks of the procedure, known as xenotransplantation, while members think about the implications. "There is a risk of passing on infections," the newspaper quoted one unnamed member of the committee as saying. "This may turn out to be a bigger problem than the ethical issue."
"We've got to be very cautious," said another.
Robin Weiss of Britain's Institute of Cancer research said he had found pig viruses could grow in human cells. "What happens if a virus, when transmitted, becomes a human epidemic?" he asked.

This is not a new fear. Scientists have warned for years that viruses were the biggest threat from animal transplants. They cite the probable origin of the AIDS virus in African monkeys as an example.

But researchers also note that heart valves from pigs have been used for years as replacements for worn-out or diseased human heart valves, and genetically altered pigs already produce insulin for treating human diabetics.

In March the Nuffield Council on Bioethics, set up by British charities to debate medical morality, said it was ethically acceptable to transplant pig organs into people, but doctors should think long and hard before doing so and should avoid using "higher" animals such as chimpanzees. One company that concentrates on possible animal-to-human transplants, Cambridge-based Imutran, said it had tested exhaustively for pig viruses and found no threat to humans.
Imutran, which was bought by Swiss pharmaceutical group Sandoz AG in April, hopes to fill a huge demand.

Earlier this year Peter Laing, drugs analyst at Salomon Brothers, said the first xenotransplants could occur in 2000 and rapidly become routine. By 2010 there could be about 250,000 a year just for kidney transplants.
An estimated 30,000 Americans and 6,000 Britons are waiting for organ transplants at any one time but fewer than half will ever receive one.
